story.logline: You scroll in bed most nights, hoping night mode protects your sleep; the scrolling, not the light, costs minutes that pile into sleep debt, so what changes if the phone goes down earlier?

question: What happens to my sleep if I stop screens before bed?

source.title: Screens before bed: what they cost your sleep
source.publisher: Test fixture written for this repo (numbers are illustrative)
quotes: Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep a night.
In one study, each hour of screen use in the hour before bed was linked to about 20 minutes less sleep that night.
People who use screens in bed also take longer to fall asleep: around 15 minutes longer on average.
If you lose 30 minutes a night, by the end of a working week you are two and a half hours short.

explain.caption: Tonight you scroll in bed. What does it cost your sleep?
You want a full night's sleep before work tomorrow.
Screen time before bed trims your sleep that night.
Screens in bed also slow how fast you fall asleep.
But dimming the screen barely helps. Putting it away does.
Sleep you needed but missed becomes sleep debt.
So small losses each night pile up across the working week.
A weekend lie-in repays only part. Your evenings decide the rest.
Now make it yours. Tell us about your evenings.

simulate.prompt: Try your own evening and watch the week's sleep debt.

tradeoffs: Evening screens can be how you relax or keep in touch, but they cost some sleep that night.
A phone outside the bedroom removes the pull to check it, but you may need another alarm clock.
A paper book or calm audio can fill the wind-down time, but a new habit takes a while to settle.
leftOut: The article calls its numbers illustrative, and the 20 and 15 minute figures are averages; your own effect may be larger or smaller.
The article gives the loss per hour of screens; the model assumes half an hour costs half as much.
The model adds the screens-before-bed and screens-in-bed effects; the article doesn't say whether they overlap, so the real total could be smaller.
A weekend lie-in pays back part of the debt, but the article gives no figure, so the model leaves it out.
Night mode helps a little, but the article gives no figure, so the model does not include it.
Stress, caffeine, noise and a regular bedtime also change sleep, and the model leaves them out.
